sweep_summary: Akan (akan1250) is in the catalog as 'tonal' on Welmers 1946 (Fanti). Of the 14 title-keyword items (12 distinct works; Anderson 2018 and Obeng 1999 each appear twice), none is a word-stress study. downloaded and read: Marfo 2003 (Internet Archive copy of the HKU proceedings; phrasal tone rules, no stress), Kügler & Genzel 2012 (open Potsdam postprint; p. 334 gives the best statement: Christaller's stress distribution is the only claim, no comprehensive analysis exists, H-tone/stress conflation may be a perceptual impression — confirms 'tonal'), Bat-El 1988 (SAL 19(2), open download; nasality on morae, stress only in an analogy). Marfo 2004 (already listed, held by the project) treats prominence as inherent to lexical tone. Abstract only: Anderson 2018 IU dissertation (speech-cycling study of rhythmic prominence — H tones, downsteps, heavy syllables; ProQuest-only full text; medium priority since his 2009 paper explicitly says Akan is not known to have a physical manifestation of stress). Paywalled/unread, low priority: Kandybowicz 2015 (syntax-phonology, prosodic vacuity), Ofori 2013 (reduplication), Purvis 2009 (praise-poetry rhythm), de Jong & Obeng 2000 (labio-palatalization, not relevant). Obeng 1999 is a Köppe monograph on conversational prosody, print only. Agyekum 2020 (emotion vocabulary) and Neeley 1997 (CD review) are noise. The catalog's classification stands; the primary first-hand stress statements for Akan remain Christaller 1875 §30 and 1933 p. XXVIII (both held by the project from the previous search), which Kügler & Genzel summarize and discount.

new_statements.quote: According to Christaller (1933) Akan has stress [...]. However, to our knowledge, no comprehensive analysis of stress exists, and the exact phonetic details of the “emphasis put on a syllable” (Christaller, 1933, p. XXVIII) remain unclear. [...] Stress in verbs can fall on the prefix or on the stem. In nouns stress lies either on the first H toned syllable, or on the preceding L toned syllable. In nouns containing only L tones the first stem syllable carries the stress, as in wɔ̀ƒà – ‘uncle’. However, assuming H tones correlate with stress may be a misleading perceptual impression. Any analysis of stress in a tone language has to be independently motivated.
new_statements.citation: Kügler, Frank & Genzel, Susanne (2012). On the prosodic expression of pragmatic prominence: The case of pitch register lowering in Akan. Language and Speech 55(3): 331-359. doi:10.1177/0023830911422182 (open postprint, Universität Potsdam phr369)
new_statements.locator: p. 334, section 1.1 (paragraph following Figure 1); text extraction lines 209-219
new_statements.reading: Akan is a terraced-level tone language; the only word-stress claim in the literature is Christaller's (1875 Grammar §30 / 1933 Dictionary p. XXVIII) impressionistic rule (nouns: first H-toned syllable or the L-toned syllable immediately before it; all-low nouns: first stem syllable; verbs: prefix or stem), which two phoneticians who worked on Akan prosody treat as unverified and possibly an artefact of H tone; no phonetic or phonological analysis of stress exists. This supports the catalog's 'tonal' coding and flags Christaller as the source of any 'has stress' reading.

sources.note: Focus-prosody study (F0 register lowering under corrective focus), but it contains an explicit first-hand assessment of word stress: the only stress claim for Akan is Christaller's impressionistic distribution (nouns: first H-toned syllable or the L-toned syllable before it; all-L nouns: first stem syllable; verbs: prefix or stem); no comprehensive phonetic/phonological analysis of stress exists and the impression may be an artefact of H tone. sources.quote: 'The accent or stress of a word is the emphatic pronunciation of a syllable ... In verbs the stress depends much on the changes of tone; it is either on prefixes, or on the stem ... In nouns with low tones throughout, the first syllable of the stem usually has the stress; e.g. wofa.' sources.quote: To uncover prominent elements and their effects on rhythmic coordination, we used the speech cycling methodology ... The units of prominence investigated were H tones (HTs), downsteps, long vowels, CRV structures, word-final and syllabic nasal consonants, and disyllabic words with varying positions of vowels with differing sonority. ... In Experiment 1, phrases with all HTs and all LTs were examined, finding no difference in coordination between these tonal patterns. ... Experiment 7 explored phrases with six syllables, finding no differences in rhythmic coordination of single HTs.
sources.locator: IUCAT record 17888452, Summary field (Dissertation Abstracts International 79-12A(E))
sources.note: Abstract never mentions stress; the 'prominent elements' studied are H tones, downsteps, long vowels and heavy syllables under speech-cycling entrainment. The author's earlier paper (Anderson 2009 IULCWP, held by the project from the previous search, conclusion) states 'Akan is not known to have a physical manifestation of stress', so the dissertation may contain a literature review of the stress question, but this could not be verified.
